issue.issue_text: Whether the extraordinary writ jurisdiction of the High Court under Articles 226/227 of the Constitution can be invoked for the release of a seized vehicle when a specific statutory remedy under the Code of Criminal Procedure, 1973 is available.

facts: The appellant's vehicle was seized under the Gujarat Prohibition Act, 1949, for allegedly carrying liquor beyond the permissible limit.

Instead of approaching the concerned criminal court under Section 451 of the Code of Criminal Procedure (Cr.P.C.) for the vehicle's release, the appellant directly filed a Special Criminal Application in the High Court under Articles 226/227 of the Constitution.
The High Court dismissed this application, leading to the appeal before the Supreme Court.
law: Section 451 of the Cr.P.C. is a specific statutory provision that empowers a criminal court to pass appropriate orders for the custody and disposal of property (like a seized vehicle) pending an inquiry or trial.
Articles 226/227 of the Constitution grant High Courts an extraordinary writ jurisdiction.
The established legal principle is that the extraordinary jurisdiction of the High Court should not be invoked when a specific and effective statutory remedy is available to the aggrieved party.
application: The Supreme Court reasoned that the appellant had a clear, specific, and adequate statutory remedy available under Section 451 of the Cr.P.C.
The appellant chose to bypass this established legal procedure and directly approached the High Court, which the Court deemed an improper course of action.
The Court held that the criminal court, which handles the trial, is the appropriate forum with the jurisdiction and power to decide on the custody of the seized property.
Invoking the High Court's extraordinary jurisdiction in such a situation undermines the specific procedural framework provided by the Cr.P.C.
reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court decided that the extraordinary writ jurisdiction of the High Court under Articles 226/227 cannot be invoked for the release of a seized vehicle when a specific statutory remedy, such as Section 451 of the Cr.P.C., is available. Therefore, the High Court was justified in dismissing the appellant's application, and the appeal was rejected.

issue.issue_text: Whether Section 98(2) of the Gujarat Prohibition Act, 1949, puts an absolute embargo on the release of a vehicle seized for carrying liquor beyond the prescribed quantity until the final judgment of the court.

facts: The appellant's vehicle was seized under the Gujarat Prohibition Act, 1949, for allegedly carrying 1240 litres of liquor, a quantity far exceeding the prescribed limit of 20 litres.

The State of Gujarat argued that Section 98(2) of the Act forbids the release of such a vehicle on bond or surety until the final judgment of the court, as the quantity of seized liquor was over the prescribed limit.
law: Section 98(2) of the Gujarat Prohibition Act states that a conveyance used for carrying liquor exceeding the prescribed quantity "shall not be released on bond or surety till the final judgement of the Court."

The Court also considered Section 132 of the Gujarat Prohibition Act and Section 451 of the Code of Criminal Procedure (Cr.P.C.), which deal with the procedure for handling seized property and the court's power to make orders for its interim custody pending trial.
application: The Supreme Court conducted a "conjoint reading" of Section 98 and Section 132 of the Gujarat Prohibition Act, along with Section 451 of the Cr.P.C.
It determined that these provisions operate in different fields. Section 98 deals with the final *confiscation* of articles, which is an order passed by the court at the conclusion of the trial.
In contrast, provisions like Section 132 of the Act and Section 451 of the Cr.P.C. govern the interim custody and release of property while the trial is pending.
The Court noted that the part of Section 98(2) creating the supposed embargo was added by a 2011 amendment and was "not very happily worded."

By interpreting these laws together, the Court reasoned that the prohibition in Section 98(2) does not override the general powers of a court to grant interim release of a seized vehicle under other provisions of law.
reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court rejected the State's argument, holding that Section 98(2) of the Gujarat Prohibition Act does not impose an absolute embargo on the interim release of a vehicle seized for carrying liquor beyond the prescribed quantity. The Court clarified that Section 98 deals with the final act of confiscation after a judgment, not the interim release of property pending trial, which is governed by other legal provisions.

cases.case_name: Sunderbhai Ambalal Desai v. State of Gujarat
cases.principle: When a specific statutory provision exists in the Code of Criminal Procedure (like Section 451) for seeking custody of property pending inquiry or trial, that remedy must be used, and a party cannot invoke the extraordinary jurisdiction of the High Court under Article 226 of the Constitution for the same purpose.

ratio_decidendi.ratio: When a specific statutory provision exists under the Criminal Procedure Code empowering a criminal court to pass orders for the custody and disposal of property pending an inquiry or trial, the extraordinary jurisdiction of the High Court under Article 226 of the Constitution cannot be invoked to seek the same relief.
obiter: When a provision uses the conjunction “but” after a comma, the part of the provision following the conjunction is to be construed as an exception or proviso to the first part.

judicial_reasoning.core_finding: The court's primary conclusion is that the appellant's direct approach to the High Court was procedurally improper. When a specific statutory remedy is available under the Code of Criminal Procedure for the release of seized property, a litigant cannot bypass that process and invoke the extraordinary writ jurisdiction of the High Court under Articles 226/227 of the Constitution.
legal_tests_applied: Principle of exhausting alternative statutory remedies: The court applied the principle that extraordinary writ jurisdiction should not be invoked when a specific and efficacious statutory remedy is available to the litigant.

Doctrine of Harmonious Construction: In interpreting Section 98(2) of the Gujarat Prohibition Act, the court stated that because the provision is not 'happily worded,' the doctrine of harmonious construction must be applied to harmonize it with other provisions of the Act and the Code of Criminal Procedure.
why_appellant_lost: The appellant, without approaching the concerned court under Section 451, Cr.P.C, directly approached the High Court by filing Special Criminal Application under Article 226/227 of the Constitution of India, which could not be said to be the proper course of action for getting the custody of the property i.e. the vehicle in question in this case.

When there is a specific statutory provision contained in the Cr.P.C. empowering the criminal court to pass appropriate order for the proper custody and disposal of the property pending the inquiry or trial, the appellant could not have invoked the extraordinary jurisdiction of the High Court under Article 226 of the Constitution of India seeking release of his vehicle.
why_respondent_won: The respondent's position that the appellant should have first approached the concerned lower court under the specific statutory remedy provided by Section 451 of the Code of Criminal Procedure was upheld by the court as the 'proper course of action'.
policy_considerations: The ruling reinforces the judicial policy of procedural propriety and the importance of following the hierarchical structure of the court system. It prevents the High Court's extraordinary jurisdiction from being used as a routine substitute for specific remedies provided by statute, thereby ensuring that specialized procedures established by the legislature are not circumvented.
